title: Blood Pressure Medication and Alcohol: Is It Safe to Drink?
excerpt: Can you drink on blood pressure medication? How alcohol and BP pills lower pressure together, a class-by-class guide, why you should never skip a dose to drink, and the warning signs that need care.
metaDescription: Can you drink on blood pressure medication? How alcohol stacks with BP pills, which drug classes are riskiest, skipping doses, and warning signs.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** most people who take blood pressure medication can have an occasional, moderate drink without a problem, as long as their doctor hasn't told them otherwise. The main risk is simple to understand. Alcohol lowers your blood pressure for a few hours after you drink, your medication lowers it too, and the two effects add up. That can leave you dizzy, lightheaded, or fainting when you stand up. The second risk is slower and easier to miss: drinking regularly raises blood pressure over time, which works directly against the reason you're taking the pill in the first place.

**The quick rules:** Ask your doctor what amount, if any, is okay with your medicine, and drink with food. Stand up slowly, especially at night and the next morning. Never skip or delay a dose so you can drink, because stopping some blood pressure drugs suddenly can make your pressure or heart rate jump. Be careful with hangover remedies, since common painkillers and decongestants can raise blood pressure or strain your kidneys. And if you're on an alpha-blocker, a nitrate, or several blood pressure drugs at once, ask your doctor before drinking at all.

> **This is not medical advice.** This guide explains how alcohol interacts with blood pressure medicines in general. It is not a substitute for advice from a doctor or pharmacist who knows your medications, doses, and health history. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist** before drinking if you recently started or changed a blood pressure medicine, take more than one, have heart, kidney, or liver disease, or have fainted before. **Call 911 or go to the emergency room** if you faint, have chest pain, trouble breathing, swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat, a very slow or irregular heartbeat, or a reading of 180/120 or higher with symptoms like a severe headache, confusion, or vision changes.

## How Alcohol and Blood Pressure Medication Interact

To understand the interaction, it helps to know that alcohol affects blood pressure in two different ways depending on the time scale.

### In the first few hours: alcohol lowers blood pressure

Alcohol widens (dilates) your blood vessels. That's why your face can feel warm and flushed after a drink. Wider vessels mean lower resistance to blood flow, so blood pressure tends to drop in the hours after drinking. Alcohol also makes you urinate more by suppressing a hormone that tells your kidneys to hold onto water, so you lose fluid. Less fluid in your blood vessels also means lower pressure.

Almost every blood pressure medication works by lowering pressure through one of the same routes: relaxing blood vessels, slowing the heart, or helping the kidneys clear salt and water. When you stack alcohol on top, the effects are **additive**. Your pressure can fall further than either one would cause alone.

The most common result is **orthostatic hypotension**, which is a plain-English way of saying your blood pressure drops when you stand up. Normally your body tightens blood vessels and speeds up your heart a little the moment you rise, so blood keeps reaching your brain. Alcohol and many blood pressure drugs both blunt that reflex. You stand up from the couch or get out of bed at 3 a.m. to use the bathroom, the room goes gray, and you have to sit back down or you fall. Falls, not the drop in pressure itself, are where many of the real injuries come from.

### Over the next day: blood pressure can rebound

Several hours after drinking, as the alcohol wears off, blood pressure often bounces back and can climb higher than your normal level. Alcohol activates the body's stress system, raises stress hormones, and disrupts sleep, all of which push pressure up. Many people notice a higher-than-usual reading the morning after a night out. We explain this pattern in detail in our guide to [high blood pressure after drinking](/never-hungover/high-blood-pressure-after-drinking).

### Over weeks and months: regular drinking raises blood pressure

This is the part that matters most for anyone being treated for high blood pressure. Drinking regularly, especially more than two drinks a day, is a well-established cause of high blood pressure. Major guidelines, including the 2017 American College of Cardiology and American Heart Association hypertension guideline, list cutting back on alcohol as one of the standard lifestyle changes for lowering blood pressure. A 2017 meta-analysis in *The Lancet Public Health* found that people who drank more than two drinks a day and cut back substantially saw meaningful drops in their blood pressure, with larger benefits in heavier drinkers.

In practice, this means heavy drinking can make your medication look like it isn't working. Some people end up on a higher dose or a second drug when the real driver was the alcohol. If your readings are stubborn, it's worth being honest with your doctor about how much you drink.

## Can You Drink Alcohol While on Blood Pressure Medication?

For most people, an occasional drink is allowed, but "allowed" depends on your medication, your dose, how well your blood pressure is controlled, and your other health conditions. The general guidance for adults who drink is no more than one drink a day for women and two for men, and many doctors suggest less for people being treated for hypertension.

A "drink" here means a standard drink: about 12 ounces of regular beer, 5 ounces of wine, or 1.5 ounces of 80-proof liquor. Restaurant wine pours, craft beers, and mixed cocktails often hold more than one standard drink, so it's easy to have "two drinks" that are really three or four.

Your risk from even a small amount of alcohol is higher if:

- You **just started** a blood pressure medicine or your dose was **recently increased**. The first days and weeks are when dizziness is most common.
- You take **two or more** blood pressure drugs, or a combination pill that contains two.
- You're **older**, since the reflex that steadies your blood pressure when you stand tends to weaken with age, and falls are more dangerous.
- You're **dehydrated** from heat, exercise, illness, or a diuretic.
- You also take other drugs that lower blood pressure or cause drowsiness, such as some medicines for prostate symptoms, erectile dysfunction, sleep, anxiety, or pain.

If none of these apply and your doctor hasn't given you a specific warning, an occasional drink with a meal is often okay, but confirm the amount with your doctor. If several apply, ask before you drink.

## Blood Pressure Medication and Alcohol: A Drug-Class Guide

Blood pressure medicines fall into a handful of families. The basic "alcohol lowers pressure too" warning applies to all of them, but each class has its own extra wrinkles. Find yours below. If you're not sure which class your pill belongs to, your pharmacist can tell you in a few seconds, and the class is usually printed on the information leaflet.

| Drug class | Common examples | Main extra concern with alcohol |
|---|---|---|
| ACE inhibitors | lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril, benazepril | Dizziness; kidney strain if dehydrated; potassium changes |
| ARBs | losartan, valsartan, olmesartan, irbesartan | Dizziness; kidney strain if dehydrated |
| Calcium channel blockers | amlodipine, nifedipine, diltiazem, verapamil | Flushing, headache, swelling; verapamil may slow alcohol clearance |
| Beta-blockers | metoprolol, propranolol, carvedilol, atenolol | Dizziness; masks a racing heart; never stop suddenly |
| Diuretics (water pills) | hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone, furosemide, spironolactone | Dehydration and electrolyte loss stack with alcohol's own fluid loss |
| Alpha-blockers | doxazosin, prazosin, terazosin | Strongest risk of fainting when standing |
| Central agents | clonidine, guanfacine, methyldopa | Extra drowsiness; dangerous rebound if doses are skipped |
| Vasodilators and nitrates | hydralazine, minoxidil, nitroglycerin, isosorbide | Sharp drops in pressure; ask your doctor before drinking |

### ACE inhibitors (lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril)

ACE inhibitors relax blood vessels by blocking a hormone system that normally tightens them and holds onto salt. With alcohol, the main issue is the extra drop in pressure and the dizziness that comes with it. Because ACE inhibitors change how the kidneys handle blood flow, getting badly dehydrated from a night of drinking (or from vomiting the next day) puts extra strain on the kidneys. They can also raise potassium levels, which matters if you also use salt substitutes or potassium supplements.

One thing worth knowing about ACE inhibitors in general: they can rarely cause **angioedema**, a sudden swelling of the lips, tongue, face, or throat. It isn't caused by alcohol, but if it happens on a night you've been drinking, don't write it off as an allergic reaction to the drink. Throat swelling is an emergency. Our full guide to [lisinopril and alcohol](/never-hungover/lisinopril-and-alcohol) goes deeper.

### ARBs (losartan, valsartan)

ARBs work on the same hormone system as ACE inhibitors, just at a different step, so the alcohol concerns are very similar: added dizziness, especially when standing, and kidney strain if you get dehydrated. ARBs are often combined with a diuretic in a single pill (for example, losartan with hydrochlorothiazide). If yours is a combination, you have two pressure-lowering effects plus a fluid-loss effect, and alcohol adds to all three. See our guides to [losartan and alcohol](/never-hungover/losartan-and-alcohol) and [valsartan and alcohol](/never-hungover/valsartan-and-alcohol).

### Calcium channel blockers (amlodipine, nifedipine, diltiazem, verapamil)

These drugs relax the muscle in blood vessel walls. Amlodipine and nifedipine mostly act on blood vessels; diltiazem and verapamil also slow the heart. Common side effects include flushing, headache, and ankle swelling, and alcohol can make the flushing and headache more noticeable, along with the dizziness.

Verapamil has one specific wrinkle: its prescribing information notes that it may increase blood alcohol levels and prolong alcohol's effects, apparently by slowing how quickly the body clears alcohol. In practice, a drink may hit harder and last longer than you expect. Our guide to [amlodipine and alcohol](/never-hungover/amlodipine-and-alcohol) covers the most commonly prescribed drug in this group.

### Beta-blockers (metoprolol, propranolol, carvedilol, atenolol)

Beta-blockers slow the heart and reduce how hard it pumps. Alcohol adds to their pressure-lowering effect and to the tiredness some people feel on them. They also blunt your heart's normal response to stress, which has two practical effects after drinking: For atenolol specifically, see our [atenolol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/atenolol-and-alcohol).

- They can **hide a racing heart**, which is one of the usual signals that you're dehydrated or that something is wrong.
- They can make it harder for your body to correct a drop in pressure when you stand up.

The most important rule with beta-blockers: **never stop them suddenly**, including skipping doses because you plan to drink. Abruptly stopping can cause a rebound surge in heart rate and blood pressure, and in people with heart disease it can trigger chest pain or worse. Carvedilol also blocks alpha receptors (see below), so it has a somewhat higher risk of dizziness when standing. Read more in our guides to [beta-blockers and alcohol](/never-hungover/beta-blockers-and-alcohol), [metoprolol and alcohol](/never-hungover/metoprolol-and-alcohol), [propranolol and alcohol](/never-hungover/propranolol-and-alcohol), and [carvedilol and alcohol](/never-hungover/carvedilol-and-alcohol).

### Diuretics, or "water pills" (hydrochlorothiazide, furosemide, spironolactone)

Diuretics lower blood pressure by making your kidneys flush out extra salt and water. Alcohol also makes you urinate more. Put them together and you can lose more fluid than you realize, which leads to dehydration, dizziness, and a low-pressure crash when you stand.

Diuretics also shift your electrolytes, the minerals like sodium, potassium, and magnesium your muscles and heart rely on. Thiazides and loop diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone, furosemide) tend to lower potassium and sodium. Heavy drinking can lower these too. Spironolactone does the opposite and can raise potassium. Either way, a night of drinking on top of a diuretic is a good reason to drink water alongside your alcohol and to avoid going to bed badly dehydrated. Our guides to [hydrochlorothiazide and alcohol](/never-hungover/hydrochlorothiazide-and-alcohol), [furosemide and alcohol](/never-hungover/furosemide-and-alcohol), and [spironolactone and alcohol](/never-hungover/spironolactone-and-alcohol) have the details.

### Alpha-blockers (doxazosin, prazosin, terazosin)

Alpha-blockers relax blood vessels strongly, and their best-known side effect is fainting or near-fainting when standing up, especially after the first dose or a dose increase. They are also prescribed for prostate symptoms and, in the case of prazosin, for nightmares, so some people don't realize they're on a blood pressure drug at all. This class has the highest risk of a serious dizziness or fainting episode when combined with alcohol. If you take one, ask your doctor before drinking, and be especially careful getting up at night. Our [prazosin and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/prazosin-and-alcohol) covers the most common one in detail.

### Central agents (clonidine, guanfacine, methyldopa)

These drugs act on the brain to lower the signals that tighten blood vessels. They commonly cause drowsiness and dry mouth, and alcohol adds to the drowsiness, so the combination can leave you more sedated and impaired than you expect. Driving after even one drink is a bad idea here. Our guides to [clonidine and alcohol](/never-hungover/clonidine-and-alcohol) and [guanfacine and alcohol](/never-hungover/guanfacine-and-alcohol) cover these medicines in detail.

Clonidine in particular should never be stopped suddenly. Missing doses can cause a dangerous rebound spike in blood pressure, sometimes with a pounding headache, agitation, and a racing heart. That's a real risk if a night of drinking leads you to forget your evening dose.

### Vasodilators and nitrates (hydralazine, minoxidil, nitroglycerin, isosorbide)

Hydralazine and minoxidil relax arteries directly and are usually added when other drugs haven't been enough, which means the people taking them are often on several blood pressure medicines already. Nitrates such as nitroglycerin and isosorbide are mainly used for chest pain (angina) rather than blood pressure, but they cause a strong drop in pressure, and their labels warn that alcohol can make that drop worse. If you use any of these, talk to your doctor before drinking.

## Should You Skip Your Blood Pressure Pill If You're Going to Drink?

No. This is one of the most common and riskiest mistakes. People sometimes skip a dose on a night out, thinking it will make drinking safer. It usually doesn't, and with some drugs it's actively dangerous:

- **Beta-blockers and clonidine** can cause a rebound jump in heart rate and blood pressure when stopped suddenly.
- **Missing doses of any blood pressure drug** leaves your pressure uncontrolled during the next-day rebound, when it may already be running higher than normal.

The safer approach is to keep taking your medication exactly as prescribed and adjust the drinking instead: fewer drinks, slower, with food and water. If you're worried about a specific night, such as a wedding, ask your doctor or pharmacist ahead of time how to handle it. They may have specific advice about timing for your medication.

## How Long After Taking Blood Pressure Medication Can You Drink?

There is no single waiting period that applies to everyone, and most blood pressure medicines don't come with one. That's because most of them are long-acting: they're designed to keep working across the full 24 hours between doses. Amlodipine, for example, stays in the body for days. With drugs like that, there's no point in the day when the medicine has "worn off," so waiting a few hours after your dose doesn't really change the interaction.

What does help:

- **Stick to your usual schedule** rather than shifting doses around alcohol.
- If you take a medicine that's known to cause dizziness a few hours after each dose (some shorter-acting drugs and alpha-blockers work this way), ask your pharmacist whether your timing matters.
- **Pay attention to how you feel** in the hours after drinking rather than counting on the clock.

If your doctor has given you specific timing advice for your medication, follow that over any general rule.

## Blood Pressure Medication, Alcohol, and the Next Morning

The morning after can bring its own interactions, often from the remedies people reach for when they're hungover.

### Painkillers: be careful with ibuprofen and naproxen

Ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin) and naproxen (Aleve) are anti-inflammatory painkillers called NSAIDs. They can raise blood pressure, they can make many blood pressure drugs less effective, and they can strain the kidneys, especially when you're dehydrated. Doctors are particularly cautious about combining an NSAID with an ACE inhibitor or ARB **and** a diuretic, a combination sometimes called the "triple whammy" because of its risk to the kidneys. A dehydrated hangover morning is exactly the setting where that risk is highest.

An occasional single dose may be fine for some people, but ask your pharmacist which painkiller suits you. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) doesn't raise blood pressure the same way, though it has its own liver concerns with alcohol, which we cover in our [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) guide. Our [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) guide covers the stomach and kidney side of NSAIDs.

### Decongestants and "cold and sinus" products

Decongestants like pseudoephedrine and phenylephrine narrow blood vessels and can raise blood pressure. They're common in cold, sinus, and some multi-symptom products. If you have high blood pressure, check labels and ask a pharmacist before using them. Our guide to [Advil Cold and Sinus and alcohol](/never-hungover/advil-cold-and-sinus-and-alcohol) explains the issue with one popular product.

### Caffeine, salty food, and dehydration

Strong coffee, energy drinks, and a salty fried breakfast can all push your blood pressure up a bit. None of these is dangerous in normal amounts, but combined with a post-drinking rebound, your morning reading may be higher than usual. Water, a normal meal, and some rest usually help more than anything else.

### Checking your blood pressure after drinking

If you have a home monitor, it's reasonable to check your pressure the morning after, but don't panic over one high reading. Sit quietly for five minutes, check again, and look at the trend over several days rather than a single number. If readings are consistently high, or you get a very high reading with symptoms, follow the warning-sign guidance below.

## Warning Signs: When to Get Help

Most problems from mixing alcohol and blood pressure medication are mild and pass with rest, water, and food. Some are not.

**Sit or lie down, and call your doctor or pharmacist, if you have:**

- Dizziness or lightheadedness that keeps coming back when you stand
- Unusual weakness, tiredness, or confusion
- Muscle cramps or weakness, which can be a sign of an electrolyte problem on a diuretic
- Blood pressure readings that are much lower or higher than your normal for more than a day

**Call 911 or go to the emergency room if you have:**

- Fainting, or a fall where you hit your head
- Chest pain, shortness of breath, or a very slow, very fast, or irregular heartbeat
- Swelling of the lips, tongue, face, or throat, or trouble swallowing or breathing
- A reading of 180/120 or higher together with symptoms such as a severe headache, chest pain, shortness of breath, confusion, weakness, or vision changes. The American Heart Association describes this as a hypertensive emergency.
- Signs of a stroke: face drooping, arm weakness, or slurred speech

If you get a reading of 180/120 or higher with no symptoms, wait five minutes and check again. If it's still that high, contact your doctor promptly.

## Practical Tips for Drinking Safely on Blood Pressure Medication

If your doctor is fine with you having the occasional drink, these habits lower the risk:

1. **Count standard drinks honestly.** Stay within the amount your doctor okayed, and remember one large pour can be two drinks.
2. **Eat before and while you drink.** Food slows how fast alcohol reaches your bloodstream and blunts the pressure swing.
3. **Alternate with water.** This matters most if you take a diuretic.
4. **Stand up slowly.** Sit on the edge of the bed for a minute before getting up at night, and hold onto something stable.
5. **Don't drive.** Even one drink plus a medicine that makes you drowsy or dizzy can affect your reactions.
6. **Keep taking your medication** exactly as prescribed. Don't skip doses to make room for a drink.
7. **Check hangover remedies with a pharmacist,** especially painkillers and anything for colds or sinus congestion.
8. **Watch the long-term pattern.** If your readings are creeping up, tell your doctor how much you drink. Cutting back may lower your blood pressure enough to matter.

## What About DHM and Other Hangover Supplements?

People often ask whether hangover supplements are safe alongside blood pressure medication. The honest answer is that very little research has looked at this question directly.

**DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that's been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the evidence comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data. There is no good evidence on how DHM interacts with blood pressure medicines in people, and some lab research suggests it may affect liver enzymes that process certain drugs, so it's reasonable to treat that as an open question. There is also no good evidence that DHM makes alcohol safer to combine with blood pressure medication, and it does nothing to reduce the additive drop in blood pressure. If you want to try it, show the product label to your pharmacist first. Our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers what is and isn't known.

If your pharmacist gives the okay, common options include [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), a simple single-ingredient capsule, and [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20). Single-ingredient products make it easier to know exactly what you're taking. Some multi-ingredient hangover blends include extra caffeine, herbs, or high doses of other compounds, which adds more unknowns for someone on heart or blood pressure medication. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains typical amounts.

For most people on blood pressure medication, the most effective hangover strategy is also the simplest: drink less, drink slower, and eat and hydrate well. Our guide to [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence, and our broader guide to [alcohol and hypertension](/never-hungover/alcohol-hypertension-blood-pressure-management-2025) explains how drinking fits into long-term blood pressure control.

## The Bottom Line

- Alcohol lowers blood pressure for a few hours, and blood pressure medicines do too. Together they can cause dizziness and fainting, especially when you stand up.
- Regular drinking raises blood pressure over time and can make your medication look less effective. Cutting back is one of the standard ways to lower blood pressure.
- Many people on a single, stable medication can have an occasional drink with food, but the amount should come from your doctor, especially if you take several drugs, an alpha-blocker, a nitrate, or recently started or changed a dose.
- Never skip doses to drink. Beta-blockers and clonidine in particular can cause dangerous rebound effects when stopped suddenly.
- Be careful with hangover remedies. NSAIDs and decongestants can raise blood pressure or strain the kidneys.
- Fainting, chest pain, throat swelling, or a reading of 180/120 or higher with symptoms means emergency care, not waiting it out.

For how alcohol interacts with other common prescriptions beyond blood pressure drugs, see our [alcohol and medications guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-medications).

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking blood pressure medication?**

Most people can have an occasional, moderate drink while on blood pressure medication, unless their doctor has told them not to. The main risk is that alcohol and the medicine both lower blood pressure, which can cause dizziness or fainting, especially when standing up. Let your doctor set the amount, drink with food, stand up slowly, and ask your doctor first if you take several blood pressure drugs or recently started or changed a dose.

**What happens if you mix alcohol and blood pressure pills?**

In the first few hours, the combination usually lowers your blood pressure more than either would alone. That can cause lightheadedness, dizziness, tiredness, or fainting, particularly when you stand up quickly. Later, as the alcohol wears off, blood pressure can rebound higher than normal. Over weeks and months, regular drinking raises blood pressure and works against the medication.

**Should I skip my blood pressure medication if I'm going to drink?**

No. Skipping doses is usually riskier than taking the medicine as prescribed. Stopping beta-blockers or clonidine suddenly can cause a dangerous rebound in heart rate and blood pressure, and missing any blood pressure medicine leaves your pressure uncontrolled during the next-day rebound. Keep your normal schedule and drink less instead. If you're worried about a specific event, ask your doctor or pharmacist ahead of time.

**How long after taking blood pressure medication can I drink alcohol?**

There's no standard waiting period for most blood pressure medicines, because they're designed to work across the full day between doses. Waiting a few hours after your pill doesn't really avoid the interaction. Stick to your normal dosing schedule, limit how much you drink, and ask your pharmacist if your specific medicine has timing advice.

**Which blood pressure medications are most dangerous with alcohol?**

Alpha-blockers (such as doxazosin, prazosin, and terazosin) have the highest risk of fainting when combined with alcohol. Nitrates and direct vasodilators can also cause sharp drops in pressure. Central agents like clonidine add drowsiness, and diuretics add to alcohol's dehydrating effect. Taking two or more blood pressure drugs at once also raises the risk. Your doctor or pharmacist can tell you how your specific medicines rank.

**Can alcohol make blood pressure medication stop working?**

A single drink doesn't stop your medicine from working. But drinking regularly, especially more than two drinks a day, raises blood pressure over time and can make it look as if your medication isn't working. Some people end up needing higher doses or extra drugs because of drinking. Cutting back often brings readings down.

**Is it safe to take ibuprofen for a hangover if I'm on blood pressure medication?**

Be cautious. Ibuprofen and naproxen can raise blood pressure, reduce how well many blood pressure drugs work, and strain the kidneys, especially when you're dehydrated after drinking. The risk is highest if you take an ACE inhibitor or ARB together with a diuretic. Ask your pharmacist which painkiller suits you, drink water, and eat something first.

**Is DHM safe with blood pressure medication?**

There is no good evidence either way on how DHM interacts with blood pressure medicines in people, and it does not make alcohol safer to combine with them. Some lab research suggests DHM may affect liver enzymes that process certain drugs. If you want to try it, show the label to your pharmacist first and choose a single-ingredient product so you know exactly what you're taking.
